items.title: 7.2.2 Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction

source_refs.note: Topic 7.2.2, printed pages 147-148 (Figure 7.2 and Table 7.1), with Quick Check 7.3 as the self-check. The print's 0.04 / 100 = 4 x 10^-4 does not fit its graph or Table 7.1; the tangent gives about 2.5 x 10^-4.

blocks.text: Measuring the rate of a reaction means determining the concentration of a reactant or product at regular intervals as the reaction progresses. A graph of concentration (y-axis) against time (x-axis) gives a curve. For the decomposition of HI to H2 and I2 at 500 degrees C the data of Table 7.1 give a falling curve, since HI is a reactant. The steepness of the curve reflects the progress of the reaction: the greater the slope near the start, the greater the rate. To measure the rate at, say, 100 seconds, draw a tangent to the curve there and measure its slope: complete a right-angled triangle with the tangent as hypotenuse; the tangent at 100 s falls by 0.04 mol dm-3 over about 160 s, so rate = 0.04 / 160 = 2.5 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 s-1. This means the HI concentration is decreasing by about 2.5 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 every second at that moment. A graph of the concentration of a product, H2 or I2, gives a rising curve whose tangent at 100 s gives the same rate.

blocks.alt: A graph of [HI] against time from 0 to 350 s with the points of Table 7.1 (0.100 at 0 s falling to 0.0265 at 350 s) on a smooth falling curve. A blue tangent touches the curve at 100 s; a red right-angled triangle under it shows a fall of 0.04 mol dm-3 over about 160 s, so the rate at 100 s is about 2.5 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 s-1.
